----------------------------------------------------------------
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
   • Primary design: Instrumental-Variables Local Projections (LP-IV) / narrative event-study.  
   • Rationale  
     – Government spending (G) is jointly determined with the business cycle, so an OLS regression of GDP on G is biased.  
     – We can exploit “narrative” or “surprise” fiscal shocks – i.e., the component of quarterly changes in government spending that was unexpected by agents and policy-makers at the time (Romer-Romer-style, IMF WEO forecast errors, or real-time budget surprises).  
     – These shocks are predetermined with respect to contemporaneous output (because they are measured before GDP for the current quarter is released) and therefore satisfy the exclusion restriction.  
     – Using them as instruments for Δ G allows causal estimation of the impulse-response profile of GDP to a one-off fiscal surprise.  
   • Empirical model  

       Step 1 (first stage):  
            ΔG_t = π Z_t  + controls_t + ε_t  

       Step 2 (second stage, horizon h):  
            Δy_{t+h} = β_h Ĝ_t + controls_{t} + u_{t+h}  

       where Z_t is the fiscal-shock instrument and Ĝ_t the fitted value from the first stage. Running this for h = 0,…,12 (three years) yields short- and long-run effects.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
   • Treatment variable – unexpected ("exogenous") change in real government purchases, Z_t. Possible constructions:  
       (i) Narrative dummy taking value 1 in quarters identified by policy documents as exogenous spending increases (defense buildups, disaster spending, etc.) and 0 otherwise; or  
       (ii) Continuous shock = (actual G – one-step-ahead forecast of G obtained from contemporary official forecasts).  
   • Control (counterfactual) – quarters with Z_t = 0 (or, in continuous formulation, quarters with small/no shock).  
   • Timing – event date is quarter t in which the shock occurs. Impulse responses trace outcomes up to h = 12 quarters afterward.  
   • No running variable or cutoff (not an RDD).

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
   A1. Relevance: Z_t is correlated with contemporaneous ΔG_t (instrument strong). Plausible because narrative shocks are defined precisely as large, discrete spending changes.  
   A2. Exclusion: Z_t affects GDP only through its impact on government spending, not via other simultaneous channels (e.g., monetary policy). The narrative design, use of real-time information, and control covariates (interest rates, taxes) make this credible.  
   A3. No anticipation: Agents cannot perfectly foresee the shocks; otherwise GDP might react prior to t. Plausible for many military or disaster events, testable with lead terms.  
   A4. Stable shock process: The interpretation of Z_t as “exogenous” is time-invariant across decades. We will test robustness over sub-samples.  
   A5. Linear projection validity: The local-projection coefficients β_h correctly approximate impulse responses if the economy is weakly stationary.

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
   1. Weak instruments (small or noisy shocks)  
        – Compute first-stage F-statistic; collapse multiple sources into a single principal-component shock series to raise signal-to-noise; report LIML & Anderson‐Rubin CIs.  
   2. Policy confounding (monetary policy moves together with fiscal shocks)  
        – Control for high-frequency monetary-policy surprises, add Fed funds futures shocks, include lagged inflation & output gaps; re-estimate excluding monetary-policy reaction quarters.  
   3. Anticipation or reverse causality  
        – Include 4 leads of Z_t in second stage; absence of pre-trends supports no-anticipation.  
        – Use alternative forecast sources (Survey of Professional Forecasters, OECD) to ensure contemporaneous information set.

5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# -------- 0. Packages ----------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # fast IV and panel regressions
library(readr)

# -------- 1. Load Data ---------
df <- read_csv("quarterly_macro.csv")   # must contain date, g, gdp, shock_raw, controls

# -------- 2. Variable Construction ----------
df <- df %>% 
  arrange(date) %>% 
  mutate(
    dG   = 100 * (log(g)    - lag(log(g))),        # %Δ government spending
    dGDP = 100 * (log(gdp)  - lag(log(gdp))),      # %Δ real GDP
    shock = shock_raw / lag(g),                    # scale shock (optional)
    year  = lubridate::year(date),
    qtr   = lubridate::quarter(date)
  ) %>% 
  drop_na()

# -------- 3. First-Stage Strength Check ----------
first_stage <- feols(dG ~ shock + lags(dG, 4) + lags(dGDP, 4) | 0, data = df)
summary(first_stage)$ivfstat   # Kleibergen-Paap F-stat

# -------- 4. Local-Projection loop (IV) ----------
horizons <- 0:12   # 0-to-3-years
lp_iv <- map_df(horizons, function(h){
  df_h <- df %>% mutate(dGDP_lead = lead(dGDP, h))
  est <- feols(dGDP_lead ~ 1 | shock + lags(dG,4) + lags(dGDP,4),
               data = df_h, iv = ~ shock)
  tibble(h = h,
         beta = coef(est)[1],
         se   = se(est)[1])
})

# -------- 5. Robustness: alternative shock measure ----------
df_alt <- df %>% mutate(shock_alt = shock_raw_alt / lag(g))
est_alt <- feols(dGDP ~ 1 | shock_alt + lags(dG,4) + lags(dGDP,4),
                 data = df_alt, iv = ~ shock_alt)

# -------- 6. Plot IRF ----------
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(lp_iv, aes(x = h, y = beta)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = beta - 1.96*se, ymax = beta + 1.96*se)) +
  labs(title = "IV Local Projections: Response of GDP to a 1-ppt Spending Shock",
       x = "Quarters after shock", y = "% change in GDP")
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
Economic theory (Keynesian and neoclassical models with less-than-unitary crowd-out) suggests a positive short-run multiplier: a 1 pp-of-GDP exogenous spending increase should raise real GDP by roughly 0.8–1.5 pp within 4 quarters. Over 3–5 years, effects should fade or even reverse as debt accrues; hence β_h expected to decline to ≈ 0 by h ≈ 12.

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV design)  
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) …………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion (no other direct channels) …………………… 0.8  
C3: No anticipation / pre-trend balance …………………… 0.8  
C4: Sample stability & no structural breaks ………………… 0.6  
C5: Correct inference (heteroskedasticity-robust, HAC) … 1  
Overall (average) ≈ 0.84 → design appears credible but still requires careful robustness exploration.

----------------------------------------------------------------
